gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Tesla's NEMA adapters are tied to the Mobile Connector generation (AC Works: Gen 1 Tesla adapters no longer fit the Gen 2 Mobile Connector), or that an adapter plugged into a Tesla adapter (for example a 14-30-to-14-50 pigtail on Tesla's 14-50 adapter) does not lower the Mobile Connector's current. The connector sets its amps from the Tesla adapter it sees, so it would draw the 14-50 rate on a 30 A dryer circuit.
standout_why: I compared against plugandrange.com/portable-chargers/nema-14-30 and thechargecurve.com/home-ev-chargers/best-nema-14-30, the two top dryer-outlet buying guides, and against the cited help.getneocharge.com adapters page. The Charge Curve says only that 'adapters made for the Gen 2 Mobile Connector let it plug into a 14-30 outlet' and never names Gen 1 or a newer connector. Plug & Range does not cover Mobile Connector generations at all. NeoCharge says its adapters 'automatically reduce your charge rate to 24 Amps' but names no generation and no exclusions. ChatGPT's own answer already tells shoppers to avoid generic 14-30-to-14-50 adapters, so the stacking warning only partly closes a gap. Both rivals already cover the J1772-vs-NACS pairing and the adapter a NACS EVDANCE needs for a J1772 car, plus the Grizzl-E Mini's included 14-30P adapter and its 24 A DIP-switch cap. So this finding partly overlaps what is already out there.
decides: This confirms the Tesla pick rather than changing it. The Tesla row should say the dryer-outlet setup is a Gen 2 Mobile Connector plus a Gen 2 (or Gen 2-compatible) 14-30 or 10-30 adapter that plugs straight into the connector. Stacking a pigtail on the 14-50 adapter, or using a Gen 1 adapter, is excluded. That suits a Tesla owner who already has a Gen 2 connector. For J1772 cars it leaves the EVDANCE 14-30 J1772 (native plug, no adapter) as the simpler pick, because nothing sits between the plug and the charger that could set the wrong current.
